title: Connecting an app to a database
summary: Network, volume and configuration together, plus the classic mistakes and how to read them.

steps.title: The whole picture
body: A working API plus database needs all three pieces from this module:
```text
docker network create shop
docker run -d --name db --network shop \
-e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev -e POSTGRES_DB=shop \
-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17
docker run -d --name api --network shop -p 8080:8080 \
-e ConnectionStrings__Default="Host=db;Port=5432;Database=shop;Username=postgres;Password=dev" \
acme/api:1.0
host :8080 ─▶ api ── db:5432 ──▶ db ──▶ volume pgdata
- **network** so `db` resolves;
- **volume** so the data survives the container;
- **configuration by environment**, so the same image works against any database.
In .NET, a double underscore in an environment variable name becomes `:` in configuration, so `ConnectionStrings__Default` is what `builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")` reads.

steps.prompt: Which .NET configuration key does this environment variable set? Type the key.
steps.explain: Every `__` becomes `:`. Colons are not allowed in environment variable names on all platforms, which is why .NET uses the double underscore.

steps.prompt: The API container starts at the same moment as Postgres and crashes with `Connection refused` to `db:5432`; a restart a few seconds later works. What is going on?
options: Postgres was still initialising and not accepting connections yet; the app needs to wait or retry
The DNS name `db` only becomes valid after a restart
Port 5432 must be published for the API to connect
The volume was locked by the first container
steps.explain: "Container started" is not "service ready". Retry with back-off in the app, and in Compose use a healthcheck with `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`.

steps.prompt: Match each error to its most likely cause.
pairs: the API is not on the same user-defined network as db
the connection string says localhost, which is the API container itself
the volume was initialised earlier with a different POSTGRES_PASSWORD
`Connection refused` only during the first seconds
steps.explain: The third one bites everyone: `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` is only applied when the data directory is **empty**. An existing volume keeps the old password.

steps.title: localhost is not your laptop
body: Inside a container, `localhost` / `127.0.0.1` is **the container itself**. Three common situations:
| the app runs | the database runs | Host to use |
| in a container | in a container on the same network | the container or service name: `db` |
| in a container | on your host (installed locally) | `host.docker.internal` (Docker Desktop; on Linux add `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway`) |
| on your host (`dotnet run`) | in a container with `-p 5433:5432` | `localhost`, port `5433` |
A connection string that works with `dotnet run` (localhost:5433) will **not** work once the app is containerised. Keep it in configuration, not in code, and set it per environment.

steps.prompt: Will the data still be there after `docker rm -f db` and a fresh `docker run` with the same flags?
items: Tables in a named volume `pgdata` mounted at the data directory
Tables in the container's writable layer (no `-v`)
Files in a bind-mounted host folder
Data in an anonymous volume from `-v /var/lib/postgresql/data`
steps.explain: The anonymous volume survives `rm` (unless `-v`), but a new `docker run` creates a **new** anonymous volume, so the new container cannot see the old data. Name your volumes.

steps.prompt: The API works with `dotnet run` but, containerised on network `shop`, fails to reach the database at `Host=localhost;Port=5433`. What is the right fix?
options: Set the connection string by environment for the container: `Host=db;Port=5432`
Publish port 5433 on the API container too
Run the API container with `--network host` everywhere
steps.explain: Configuration differs per environment; the image should not. `--network host` hides the problem on Linux and does not behave the same on Docker Desktop.

steps.prompt: Complete the command that runs the API against the `db` container.

steps.title: Fix "connection refused" to the database
prompt: This terminal has a **real Docker Engine**. The database container `db` (it answers like PostgreSQL on port 5432)
is on the network `shop`. The API container `api` (image `shop/api:3.0`, configured by `DB_HOST` and `DB_PORT`)
keeps logging an error: `docker logs api`.
Run a fixed `api` (same name, same image) so that its newest log line says `connected to ...:5432`.

checks.name: the API logs that it is connected
checks.fail: The API's newest log line is not `connected to ...`. `docker logs api` shows what it tries to reach.

checks.name: it runs from shop/api:3.0 on the shop network
checks.fail: There should be a running `api` from `shop/api:3.0` attached to the `shop` network (only).

checks.name: DB_HOST is not localhost
checks.fail: `DB_HOST` still points at localhost: inside a container that is the container itself.

hints: `docker inspect -f '{{json .Config.Env}}' api` and `docker inspect -f '{{json .NetworkSettings.Networks}}' api` show its configuration.
Two things are wrong: `localhost` inside a container is the container itself, and `api` is not on the network `db` is on.
`docker rm -f api`, then `docker run -d --name api --network shop -e DB_HOST=db shop/api:3.0`.
solution: docker run -d --name api --network shop -e DB_HOST=db shop/api:3.0
steps.explain: "Connection refused to localhost" from a container almost always means the app is talking to itself: each container has its own network namespace and its own `127.0.0.1`. The database is reached by its **name** on a **shared** network, which is exactly what Compose sets up for you, so `Host=db` in a connection string just works there.
